content.text:
1) Answer

Short answer: There is strong, verifiable evidence across Keir Starmer’s legal career, tenure as Director of Public Prosecutions, and current premiership that he values human rights.

Evidence:
- Lifelong human‑rights practice and scholarship before politics
  - He co‑founded and worked at Doughty Street Chambers, a set known for human rights and civil liberties work; the chambers record him overturning death sentences in Commonwealth countries and acting in major free‑speech cases. ([doughtystreet.co.uk](https://www.doughtystreet.co.uk/news/doughty-street-chambers-congratulates-sir-keir-starmer-victory-general-election?utm_source=openai))
  - He authored European Human Rights Law (a practitioner text on the Human Rights Act and ECHR) and wrote on the ECHR for Cambridge University Press, indicating subject‑matter expertise and advocacy for applying rights in UK courts. ([lag.org.uk](https://www.lag.org.uk/shop/book-title/201294/european-human-rights-law?utm_source=openai))

- Human‑rights–inflected prosecutorial policy as DPP (2008–2013)
  - He issued the assisted‑suicide prosecution policy (2010) that centres the public‑interest test on compassion and individual autonomy, following public consultation after Purdy. That policy remains the CPS framework. ([cps.gov.uk](https://www.cps.gov.uk/legal-guidance/suicide-policy-prosecutors-respect-cases-encouraging-or-assisting-suicide?utm_source=openai))
  - He introduced the Victims’ Right to Review (2013), giving victims a formal route to challenge CPS decisions not to prosecute—an institutional reform to strengthen victims’ rights in the justice system. ([itv.com](https://www.itv.com/news/story/2013-06-05/victim-initiative-cps-keir-starmer/?utm_source=openai))

- Clear, binding commitments in government to the European human‑rights system
  - Labour’s 2024 manifesto pledged: “Britain will unequivocally remain a member of the European Convention on Human Rights.” That is now the governing party’s formal policy. ([labour.org.uk](https://labour.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/Labour-Party-manifesto-2024.pdf))
  - As Prime Minister (22 July 2024), he told Parliament there is “no need to withdraw from the [ECHR]… we will not withdraw—not now, not ever,” a categorical commitment on the record in Hansard. ([hansard.parliament.uk](https://hansard.parliament.uk/html/commons/2024-07-22/CommonsChamber?utm_source=openai))

- Concrete executive action aligned with rights concerns in asylum policy
  - On taking office, he ended the Rwanda deportation scheme—criticised by the UK Supreme Court and rights groups—calling it a costly “gimmick” that would not deter crossings. Ending the scheme was one of his first decisions as PM. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/world/uk/new-uk-pm-starmer-confirms-end-rwanda-asylum-deportation-scheme-2024-07-06/?utm_source=openai))

- Balancing enforcement with rights while upholding core guarantees
  - Amid migration pressures, he has said government will review how courts apply some ECHR provisions (e.g., Articles 3 and 8) to improve removals, but has simultaneously reaffirmed UK membership of the ECHR. This indicates a law‑and‑order stance that does not abandon foundational rights commitments. ([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/law/2025/oct/01/keir-starmer-human-rights-law-echr-nigel-farage-small-boat-crossings?utm_source=openai))


2) Sources considered TRUSTWORTHY (and why)

- [1] Source: UK Parliament Hansard (Commons)
  - [2] Reasoning 1: Official verbatim parliamentary record; primary source; rigorous editorial standards.
  - [3] Reasoning 2: Direct transcript of Starmer’s “not now, not ever” ECHR commitment on 22 July 2024. ([hansard.parliament.uk](https://hansard.parliament.uk/html/commons/2024-07-22/CommonsChamber?utm_source=openai))

- [1] Source: Labour Party Manifesto 2024 (official PDF)
  - [2] Reasoning 1: Primary party document; definitive statement of governing policy.
  - [3] Reasoning 2: Explicit pledge to remain a member of the ECHR; relevant to present government stance. ([labour.org.uk](https://labour.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/Labour-Party-manifesto-2024.pdf))

- [1] Source: BBC News
  - [2] Reasoning 1: UK public‑service broadcaster; strong editorial and corrections policies.
  - [3] Reasoning 2: Reported Starmer’s decision to scrap the Rwanda scheme on day one, corroborating the policy action. ([feeds.bbci.co.uk](https://feeds.bbci.co.uk/news/articles/cz9dn8erg3zo?utm_source=openai))

- [1] Source: Reuters
  - [2] Reasoning 1: Global wire service with high fact‑checking standards and minimal editorialising.
  - [3] Reasoning 2: Reported his formal announcement terminating the Rwanda plan immediately after taking office. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/world/uk/new-uk-pm-starmer-confirms-end-rwanda-asylum-deportation-scheme-2024-07-06/?utm_source=openai))

- [1] Source: Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) guidance
  - [2] Reasoning 1: Official legal policy for prosecutors; primary, authoritative source on DPP decisions.
  - [3] Reasoning 2: The assisted‑suicide policy (issued by Starmer in 2010) and current CPS overview show the compassion‑centred public‑interest test he introduced. ([cps.gov.uk](https://www.cps.gov.uk/legal-guidance/suicide-policy-prosecutors-respect-cases-encouraging-or-assisting-suicide?utm_source=openai))

- [1] Source: ITV News (2013 report)
  - [2] Reasoning 1: Major UK broadcaster with standard editorial processes.
  - [3] Reasoning 2: Contemporaneous coverage of the Victims’ Right to Review introduced under Starmer as DPP. ([itv.com](https://www.itv.com/news/story/2013-06-05/victim-initiative-cps-keir-starmer/?utm_source=openai))

- [1] Source: Doughty Street Chambers (official chambers site)
  - [2] Reasoning 1: Primary institutional profile of his pre‑politics legal work; subject‑matter experts.
  - [3] Reasoning 2: Confirms his human‑rights practice, free‑speech cases, and death‑penalty appeals. Potential positive bias, but credible for biographical facts. ([doughtystreet.co.uk](https://www.doughtystreet.co.uk/news/doughty-street-chambers-congratulates-sir-keir-starmer-victory-general-election?utm_source=openai))

- [1] Source: Legal Action Group (publisher)
  - [2] Reasoning 1: Reputable legal publisher used by practitioners.
  - [3] Reasoning 2: Confirms authorship of European Human Rights Law, evidencing sustained engagement with UK rights law. ([lag.org.uk](https://www.lag.org.uk/shop/book-title/201294/european-human-rights-law?utm_source=openai))

- [1] Source: The Guardian (law/politics reporting)
  - [2] Reasoning 1: Established national outlet with transparent sourcing; editorial lean but robust standards.
  - [3] Reasoning 2: Reported Starmer’s position to review certain ECHR interpretations while remaining in the Convention, relevant to how he balances enforcement and rights. ([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/law/2025/oct/01/keir-starmer-human-rights-law-echr-nigel-farage-small-boat-crossings?utm_source=openai))


3) Sources considered NOT TRUSTWORTHY (and why)

- [1] Source: GB News
  - [2] Reasoning 1: Partisan broadcaster with a track record of polemical framing; variable fact‑checking.
  - [3] Reasoning 2: Coverage of Starmer’s “900‑page human‑rights manual” used to argue ideological claims adds little reliable primary evidence; better corroborated by neutral/official sources (e.g., LAG, CUP). Not used. ([gbnews.com](https://www.gbnews.com/politics/martin-daubney-human-rights-keir-starmer-british-law?utm_source=openai))

- [1] Source: British Brief (britbrief.co.uk)
  - [2] Reasoning 1: Little‑known site with unclear editorial standards and provenance.
  - [3] Reasoning 2: Emotive, uncorroborated claims about Starmer’s “manual” or policy “exposés”; insufficient reliability compared with primary sources and major outlets. Not used. ([britbrief.co.uk](https://britbrief.co.uk/politics/immigration/starmer-ill-scrap-rwanda-scheme-on-day-one.html?utm_source=openai))

- [1] Source: Skwawkbox
  - [2] Reasoning 1: Hyper‑partisan blog; assertions often based on anonymous sources; mixed record on corrections.
  - [3] Reasoning 2: Claims about Starmer’s conduct in the McLibel era conflict with more authoritative records and even counter‑statements on the same site; unsuitable for evidencing human‑rights commitments. Not used. ([skwawkbox.org](https://skwawkbox.org/2023/04/17/exclusive-starmer-used-undercover-spycop-as-driver-gofer-during-mclibel-case/?utm_source=openai))

Notes:
- I prioritised primary and high‑quality secondary sources (Hansard, official policy documents, major newswires) to demonstrate actions and binding commitments that are directly probative of valuing human rights. Where debate exists over specific policies (e.g., migration enforcement), I cited coverage showing he has maintained ECHR membership while seeking operational changes—consistent with upholding core rights guarantees. ([hansard.parliament.uk](https://hansard.parliament.uk/html/commons/2024-07-22/CommonsChamber?utm_source=openai))
